# Integrative metabolism: the fed and fasted body

> *After a meal the body must store a flood of nutrients, and between meals it must live on those
> stores while keeping the brain supplied. One connected network of pathways does both, thrown
> between storing and mobilising by hormones.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Trace carbon from glucose, fatty acids and amino acids through the hub molecules of the metabolic
  map to acetyl-CoA and the TCA cycle.
- Explain why fatty acids cannot be converted to glucose, and what follows for the body in a fast.
- Explain how the insulin-to-glucagon ratio switches the liver, muscle and adipose tissue between
  storing and mobilising fuel.
- Describe the hand-off from glycogenolysis to gluconeogenesis to ketosis in a fast, and how ketones
  spare protein.
- Distinguish physiological ketosis from diabetic ketoacidosis.
- Recognise the failures of fed–fasted regulation (diabetes and alcohol-induced hypoglycaemia), the
  symptoms of hypoglycaemia and the patient at risk of refeeding syndrome.
:::

## Integrative metabolism at a glance {#sec-overview}

Once a meal has been digested and absorbed, its glucose, amino acids and fat enter the circulation
(see the [*Macronutrients*](macronutrients.qmd) and [*Digestion & Absorption*](digestion-absorption.qmd)
chapters). What is not used at once is stored, and between meals those stores are drawn on to keep
every tissue supplied, the brain above all.

Metabolism is one network with a logic. A handful of hub molecules connect its pathways, a few
irreversible steps give it direction, and two hormones from the pancreas switch it between storing
after a meal and mobilising between meals. At the depth of a map, each pathway comes down to four
facts: what goes in, what comes out, where in the cell it runs and its one control step. No separate
biochemistry course is assumed, and the full enzyme machinery is left to biochemistry proper.

## Reading the metabolic map {#sec-partA}

### Metabolic hubs and irreversible steps {#sec-map}

Metabolism looks unmanageable as a list of fifty enzymes, but almost every pathway passes through one
of five metabolic hubs, molecules or pools where pathways meet and carbon can turn several ways:

Glucose-6-phosphate (G6P)
: Glucose tagged with a phosphate as it enters a cell; a branch point of carbohydrate metabolism.

Pyruvate
: The product of glucose breakdown, and a junction where its carbon can go four ways.

Acetyl-CoA
: The common intermediate where the breakdown of all three fuels converges.

TCA cycle
: A cycle in the mitochondrion, built around oxaloacetate, that fully oxidises acetyl-CoA to CO₂;
  the final common pathway of fuel oxidation.

Amino-acid pool
: Where protein enters and leaves the map.

Four terms apply everywhere on the map:

Catabolism
: Breaking fuel down. Catabolic pathways converge on acetyl-CoA and release energy.

Anabolism
: Building and storing. Anabolic pathways diverge from the hubs, and they cost energy.

Reciprocal regulation
: The coordination of opposing pathways so that one runs while its opposite idles. Making and burning
  glucose, or building and burning fat, are never both fully on, because together they would cancel
  out in a pointless futile cycle.

ATP
: The cell's energy currency, made and spent continuously; the energy released by catabolism is
  captured as ATP (see [ATP turnover: spent, not stored](#sec-atp)).

The map also has direction, which comes from four irreversible steps that carbon can pass through but
never return by. The rest of the map is reversible, so these four steps set the way metabolism flows.
The first of them, from pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, is the reason blood glucose must be maintained from
other sources in a fast (see [Pyruvate](#sec-pyruvate)).

Build the map below one pathway at a time onto the five hubs, and watch where each new pathway
joins: that convergence is what holds the map together.

<div data-island="metabolic-map" data-src="/diagrams/metabolic-map.yml"></div>

### Glucose-6-phosphate: a branch point {#sec-g6p}

A glucose molecule entering a cell is trapped at once: it is tagged with a phosphate to make
glucose-6-phosphate, which cannot leak back out. G6P can then take one of four routes:

- It can be burned for energy: **glycolysis** splits it into two molecules of pyruvate.
- It can be stored as glycogen, the body's fast-access glucose store.
- It can be used for building, in the **pentose phosphate pathway**, which yields not ATP but
  **NADPH** (the reducing agent used to build fats and to protect against oxidative damage) and the
  ribose sugar of DNA and RNA.
- It can be exported to the blood as free glucose, a route that only the liver and kidney can take.
  This route is how blood glucose is maintained in a fast (see
  [The fasted state](#sec-fasted)).

Glycolysis runs in the cytosol (the fluid that fills the cell around its organelles) and does not need
oxygen. It has a single committed, regulated step (the enzyme phosphofructokinase-1) and yields a
little ATP directly. Pyruvate is converted to **lactate** when oxygen is scarce, as in a sprinting
muscle, or in a cell with no mitochondria (the organelles that burn fuel with oxygen), such as a red
blood cell. Making lactate regenerates the molecule glycolysis needs to keep
running, so the cell can make ATP without oxygen. Oxygen is used later, in the mitochondrion
(see [The TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation](#sec-furnace)), and not in glycolysis itself. Even
so, the belief that glycolysis consumes oxygen is the single most common one about glucose breakdown.

::: {.callout-note}
## 🔬 Food science: why anaerobic exercise burns glucose, not fat
During a sprint up a flight of stairs, muscle runs on glucose, not fat, because only glucose can be
broken down without oxygen, quickly, in the cytosol. Fat can be burned only aerobically, which is
slower. A 100 m dash is therefore fuelled by carbohydrate and a long walk increasingly by fat (see
[Fuel use during exercise](#sec-exercise)) [@statpearlsAnaerobic].
:::

### Pyruvate and the irreversible pyruvate dehydrogenase step {#sec-pyruvate}

Pyruvate sits at the end of glycolysis as a junction, and its carbon can go four ways:

- to lactate, regenerating what glycolysis needs (as above);
- to alanine, an amino acid, and so into the amino-acid pool;
- back toward glucose via oxaloacetate, the first step of making new glucose;
- forward into acetyl-CoA.

The last step, from pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, is irreversible. It is catalysed by pyruvate
dehydrogenase (PDH), and its irreversibility makes it the first and most important of the map's four
irreversible steps, with a large consequence for fasting.

::: {.callout-important}
## Why fatty acids cannot become glucose
Fatty acids are broken down into acetyl-CoA, and the step from pyruvate to acetyl-CoA is one-way, so
**fatty acids cannot be turned back into glucose**. Of a triglyceride, only the small glycerol backbone
can become glucose (see [The fasted state](#sec-fasted)). This one irreversible step is why blood
glucose must be maintained, and new glucose made, when food runs short.
:::

### Glycogen metabolism and gluconeogenesis {#sec-glucose-store}

When the diet stops supplying glucose, two sources supply it in turn.

**Glycogen, the short-term store.** Glucose is stored as glycogen, a branched chain of glucose units, in
liver and muscle. Building it (**glycogenesis**) and breaking it down (**glycogenolysis**) are
reciprocally controlled, so the store is either filling or emptying, not both. Glycogen is a
short-term store, enough for hours, not days.

**Gluconeogenesis, making glucose from scratch.** When glycogen runs low, the liver (and, later, the
kidney) builds new glucose from three raw materials: lactate, glycerol and **glucogenic** amino acids,
those whose carbon can become glucose (see [The amino-acid pool](#sec-amino)). Gluconeogenesis is often
pictured as glycolysis run backwards, but it cannot be: three of glycolysis's steps are irreversible
(three more of the map's irreversible steps), so gluconeogenesis bypasses them with four different
enzymes. Those bypass enzymes are its control points, and because glycolysis and gluconeogenesis are
reciprocally regulated, the cell does not run both at once. The raw materials are enough at the depth
of the map; the enzyme steps belong to biochemistry proper.

### Fatty-acid oxidation, synthesis and ketogenesis {#sec-fat}

Fat is the body's most energy-dense fuel, about 9 kcal/g against roughly 4 for carbohydrate or
protein, which is why long-term energy is stored as fat.

**Burning fat.** A fatty acid is carried into the mitochondrion through a single committed transport
step; inside, **β-oxidation** chops it into many molecules of acetyl-CoA (plus the electron carriers
that feed energy production). Many acetyl-CoA per fatty acid is why fat yields so much energy.

**Storing fat.** In the other direction, a committed enzyme step sends acetyl-CoA into building fatty
acids, a process that consumes the NADPH made in the pentose phosphate pathway. The switch between the
two is a clear case of reciprocal regulation: the signal that commits the cell to building fat also
blocks the transport step for burning it. A cell therefore never builds and burns fat at the same time.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Optional: the two enzymes that regulate fatty-acid oxidation and synthesis
The transport step into the mitochondrion is catalysed by CPT1 (carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1), and
the committed enzyme for building fat is acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC), whose immediate product blocks
CPT1. One reciprocal switch therefore keeps burning and building from running at once.
:::

**Ketone bodies.** Acetyl-CoA has a third fate, which matters in a long fast. When fat breakdown floods
the fasting liver with more acetyl-CoA than it can burn, the liver converts the surplus into ketone
bodies (ketones for short) and exports them for other organs to use. The liver lacks the one enzyme
needed to use ketones, so it cannot burn its own product and exports its entire output. Exported in
this way, ketones come to fuel the brain in a long fast (see [Prolonged fasting](#sec-starvation)).

### The TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation {#sec-furnace}

Acetyl-CoA, whether it came from carbohydrate, fat or protein, enters the TCA cycle (also called the
citric acid or Krebs cycle) in the mitochondrion. There it is fully oxidised to CO₂, and the energy is
captured on electron-carrier molecules. Two properties put the TCA cycle at the centre of the map. It
is the final common pathway for all three fuels. It is also **amphibolic**: its intermediates are
drawn off to build other molecules and topped up from amino acids, so it supplies biosynthesis as well
as oxidising fuel.

The electron carriers then deliver their electrons to **oxidative phosphorylation** on the inner
mitochondrial membrane. Oxidative phosphorylation makes most of the cell's ATP, and it is the step at
which oxygen is finally used, as the last acceptor of the spent electrons (which is why we breathe).

Burned all the way with oxygen, one glucose yields about 30–32 ATP; glycolysis alone, without oxygen,
yields about 2. Older textbooks give 36–38, a figure now considered an overestimate. All of these
numbers are approximate: what matters is the roughly 15-fold gap between aerobic and anaerobic yield.

### ATP turnover: spent, not stored {#sec-atp}

ATP is easily mistaken for the body's energy store, but it is an energy currency. The body holds only
seconds' to minutes' worth at any moment, yet turns over close to its own weight in ATP each day [@tornroth2008gate],
making and spending it continuously. The body's energy stores are glycogen and fat, which are converted
into ATP on demand. Not every carrier serves ATP production: NADPH, from the pentose phosphate pathway,
supplies reducing power for synthesis and antioxidant defence and is kept separate from the carriers
that generate ATP. Confusing the two is a common slip.

### The amino-acid pool: no storage protein {#sec-amino}

The fifth hub is the amino-acid pool, and it carries a warning that shapes the response to fasting:
the body has no storage protein. Unlike glycogen and fat, every protein in the body is doing a job, as
muscle, as an enzyme, as an immune cell. Using protein for fuel therefore dismantles working tissue,
which is why protein is broken down for fuel late and at a cost.

Before an amino acid can enter the map, its nitrogen must be removed, by transamination (the reaction
of the liver enzymes ALT and AST, which appear in clinical liver tests) and deamination. The liver
packages that nitrogen as urea for the kidneys to excrete. The leftover carbon skeleton then joins the
map as one of two types, and its entry point sets its fate:

| Type | Enters the map as | Can it become glucose? | How many amino acids |
|---|---|---|---|
| Glucogenic | Pyruvate or a TCA-cycle intermediate | Yes | Most are at least partly glucogenic |
| Ketogenic | Acetyl-CoA | No (it is past the irreversible step); only ketones | A few are purely ketogenic; some others are both |

The assignment of individual amino acids varies between textbooks and is not worth memorising; the
rule holds in every scheme.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a fasting person carries weeks of energy as fat. Why can't that fat keep blood glucose up?
Fatty acids are broken down to acetyl-CoA, and the step from pyruvate to acetyl-CoA is one-way, so
their carbon cannot travel back to pyruvate and on to glucose. Only the small glycerol backbone of a
triglyceride is glucogenic. In a fast, glucose must therefore be made from lactate, glycerol and
amino acids, which is why protein is drawn on.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does a red blood cell depend entirely on glucose, when muscle can burn fat?
A red blood cell has no mitochondria, so it can run only glycolysis, which takes place in the cytosol
without oxygen and ends in lactate. Fat is burned by β-oxidation inside the mitochondrion, and the TCA
cycle and oxidative phosphorylation are mitochondrial too, so none of them is open to the red cell.
Glucose is its only fuel.
:::

## Hormonal control of fuel use: fed, fasted and starved states {#sec-partB}

The pathways of the map are always in place; what changes, hour to hour, is which of them are switched
on. Two pancreatic hormones set that almost entirely: insulin and **glucagon**, the hormone that drives
the liver to release glucose. Step through the states below, from just after a meal to a
prolonged fast, and watch which organs store, burn and export fuel, and how the fuel fluxes between
them change.

<div data-island="metabolic-switch" data-src="/diagrams/metabolic-switch.yml"></div>

### The insulin-to-glucagon ratio {#sec-switch}

Fuel use is not set by a fed hormone and a fasted hormone acting alone but by the
**insulin-to-glucagon ratio**. After a meal the ratio is high, and fuel is stored; between meals it is
low, and fuel is mobilised. The classic description is that this ratio "varies inversely
with the need to make your own glucose, and is lowest in starvation" [@unger1971ratio]. Its direction
matters, not any particular value.

Insulin is often called the sugar hormone, but it is the body's principal anabolic hormone, acting on
all three macronutrients at once. It stores glucose as glycogen, stores fat and blocks its breakdown,
and builds protein, while shutting down the opposing pathways that mobilise fuel [@merheb2026insulin].
Lowering blood glucose is only one of its effects.

### The fed (absorptive) state {#sec-fed}

After a meal, insulin is high, and the liver, skeletal muscle and adipose tissue each use the pathways
of the map to store the meal:

- The liver, the main regulator of blood glucose, takes up glucose, refills its glycogen, converts the
  excess to fat that it ships out as VLDL, and receives the meal's amino acids by the portal vein.
- Skeletal muscle, the largest site of insulin-stimulated glucose uptake, takes up glucose to rebuild
  its own glycogen and takes up amino acids to build protein.
- Adipose tissue, the fat depot, takes up glucose and stores fat. **Lipoprotein lipase**, the enzyme on
  its capillaries, strips triglyceride out of circulating lipoproteins to stock the fat cell
  [@wang2009lpl], and insulin is strongly anti-lipolytic: it brakes the release of fat from the store.
  (Adipose tissue also releases leptin in proportion to its fat stores, a long-term signal that the
  brain uses to regulate appetite and body weight; see the
  [*Appetite & Weight Regulation*](appetite-weight-regulation.qmd) chapter.)

::: {.callout-note}
## GLUT4 versus GLUT2
Glucose uptake by muscle and fat surges after a meal while the liver's does not, because muscle and
fat use a different glucose transporter from the liver. Muscle and fat use **GLUT4**, which comes to
the cell surface only when insulin signals, so the meal switches their uptake on. The liver uses
**GLUT2**, which is always present and admits glucose in proportion to its concentration, with no
insulin required. Insulin still acts on the liver, but on its enzymes, telling it to store rather than
release glucose, not on its glucose transporter [@chadt2020glucose]. This one contrast explains most
of the fed-state picture.
:::

### The fasted state: maintaining blood glucose {#sec-fasted}

As blood glucose falls between meals, insulin drops and glucagon rises, and the ratio falls so that
fuel is mobilised. Glucagon leads the **counter-regulatory hormones**, the hormones that raise a
falling blood glucose, which act at different speeds:

| Hormone | Speed | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Glucagon | Rapid; the primary responder | Drives the liver to release glucose |
| Adrenaline (epinephrine) | Fast | The backup, and the critical one if glucagon fails |
| Cortisol and growth hormone | Slow | Permissive: sustain a prolonged fast, not the acute dip |

Clinically, the acute counter-regulatory response to a low blood glucose is glucagon and adrenaline,
not cortisol and growth hormone [@cryer1993counterreg; @rizza1979].

In a fast, almost every tissue that can burn fat switches to it, leaving the scarce glucose for the two
consumers that depend on it, the brain and the red blood cell. This is **glucose sparing**. The red
blood cell has no mitochondria, so it can run only glycolysis and must have glucose. The brain also
depends on glucose. A widely taught explanation for this dependence is that fatty acids cannot cross
into the brain, but that is not the reason: fatty acids are a poor brain fuel, because they travel
bound to albumin and neurons oxidise them poorly [@schonfeld2013].

Glucose supply in a fast follows an order: glycogenolysis first, gluconeogenesis second. Liver
glycogen covers roughly the first 12–24 hours; as it runs down, gluconeogenesis takes over, building
glucose from lactate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids [@statpearlsGlycogenolysis;
@statpearlsGngPhys]. Meanwhile **lipolysis**, the breakdown of stored fat, becomes the main fuel supply
for the other tissues. Adipose tissue releases two products: fatty acids, which fuel muscle, heart and
liver; and glycerol, the one glucogenic part of fat, which feeds gluconeogenesis [@statpearlsLipolysis].

::: {.callout-important}
## Why muscle glycogen cannot raise blood glucose
Muscle holds most of the body's glycogen, yet it cannot donate a single glucose molecule to the blood.
The reason is one missing enzyme: muscle lacks **glucose-6-phosphatase**, the enzyme that frees glucose
for export, so muscle glycogen is trapped for muscle's own use. Only the liver and kidney can release
free glucose to the blood. Muscle helps indirectly, by exporting lactate, which the liver rebuilds into
glucose (the **Cori cycle**), or alanine, which carries both carbon and nitrogen to the liver (the
**glucose–alanine cycle**). The liver is the main source of glucose released into the blood; muscle
supplies only raw material for gluconeogenesis [@statpearlsGlycogenolysis].
:::

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-cori
%%| fig-cap: "Muscle cannot release glucose, so it sends carbon to the liver instead: lactate (Cori cycle) and alanine (which also carries nitrogen for disposal as urea)."
flowchart LR
  M["Muscle / red cell<br/>(no glucose export)"] -->|"lactate"| L["Liver<br/>makes glucose"]
  M -->|"alanine (carbon + nitrogen)"| L
  L -->|"glucose"| M
  L -.->|"nitrogen → urea"| U["Kidney<br/>excretes urea"]
```

### Prolonged fasting: ketosis and protein sparing {#sec-starvation}

After about a day without food, blood glucose is being maintained partly by breaking down protein for
gluconeogenesis, and protein is working tissue; left unchecked, a long fast would consume the body's
own muscle. Ketone production limits this loss.

The body's fuel reserves are of three very different kinds:

| Store | Rough size | Character |
|---|---|---|
| Glycogen | ~a day's worth of energy | Small, rapidly mobilised, used first |
| Fat | ~weeks to months | The vast bulk of stored energy |
| Protein | not a designed store at all | Functional tissue; spending it dismantles working tissue |

The exact figures vary by source and by method of counting, so they are best read as ranges that
show a shape: fat dwarfs the other reserves, glycogen is small by comparison, and protein is
not really available at all [@cahill2006fuel; @bergStryerFuel].

Fasting is a staged hand-off, often described as the **Cahill phases**. The fed state gives way to the
post-absorptive state, which runs on glycogen, and then to early fasting, which runs on
gluconeogenesis. Over days to weeks metabolism moves into protein-sparing **ketosis**, a raised level
of ketones in the blood. The metabolic switch interactive above steps through the same four states.

As the fasting liver floods with acetyl-CoA from fat breakdown, it makes ketones (β-hydroxybutyrate,
acetoacetate and the exhaled acetone) and exports them, since it cannot use them itself
[@statpearlsKetogenesis]. Unlike fatty acids, which travel bound to albumin and are a poor brain fuel,
ketones are water-soluble and readily burned by the brain. Over days to weeks the brain shifts most
of its energy supply from glucose to ketones. Less
glucose demand means less gluconeogenesis, and so less protein broken down, which stretches survival
from weeks toward months. The brain's shift to ketones refutes the common statement that the brain
can use only glucose.

::: {.callout-warning}
## How solid are the starvation numbers?
The classic figures (the brain drawing well over half its energy from ketones, and brain glucose use
falling roughly threefold) trace to a small, careful study of **three fasting volunteers with obesity**
(Owen and colleagues, 1967) and the body of work around it [@owen1967brain; @cahill2006fuel]. They are
foundational and directionally right, but they are approximate trends, not modern large-trial
constants. The brain's shift to ketones is real and large, but the precise percentages rise gradually
over days to weeks rather than snapping to a fixed value.
:::

The three ketone bodies are small molecules, and "ketone body" is a loose label: β-hydroxybutyrate is
chemically a hydroxy-acid. Acetone is the volatile one, smelt on the breath of someone deep in ketosis
or in the emergency described next. Rotate them below.

<div data-island="molecule" data-src="/structures/ketone-bodies.mol.yml"></div>

### Physiological ketosis and diabetic ketoacidosis {#sec-dka}

Because the two words sound alike, the ketosis of a fast or a ketogenic diet is easily confused with
**diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)**, a medical emergency, and a patient starting a ketogenic diet may fear
it. The two states differ in their setting, their insulin, their ketone level and their blood pH:

|  | Physiological (nutritional) ketosis | Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) |
|---|---|---|
| Setting | A fast or a ketogenic diet | Almost total absence of insulin, classically in type 1 diabetes |
| Insulin | The residual insulin the person still makes restrains fat breakdown and ketone production | Almost absent, so fat breakdown and ketone production run away |
| Ketones | A modest rise: roughly 0.5–3 mmol/L on a ketogenic diet, higher in prolonged starvation | High; the ranges can overlap with deep nutritional ketosis |
| Blood pH | Normal | Acidic |

A person in DKA usually has a very high blood glucose (hyperglycaemia) as well.

::: {.callout-important}
## The discriminator is the acidosis, not the ketone number
DKA is easily assumed to be simply very high ketones, but the ketone ranges of deep nutritional ketosis
and mild DKA overlap. What defines DKA is the acidosis, an acidic blood pH with a high anion gap (a
sign of extra acids in the blood), driven by uncontrolled insulin deficiency, not the ketone
concentration alone [@kolb2021ketones; @sheikhali2008bhb]. The molecules are the same; the difference
is the regulatory context and the blood pH. **A healthy person on a ketogenic diet does not develop
DKA, because they still make insulin.** Recognising DKA is the task at this stage; managing it belongs
to clinical training.
:::

### Refeeding syndrome {#sec-refeeding}

**Refeeding syndrome** is a dangerous fall in blood minerals when a severely malnourished or starved
person is fed again. The sudden insulin surge drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium rapidly into
cells, and blood levels can crash; the fall in phosphate (**hypophosphataemia**) is the most dangerous
and can be fatal. The task at this stage is to recognise the patient at risk: the long-starved, the
very underweight, the person who has eaten little for many days (see the
[*Undernutrition & Malnutrition*](undernutrition-malnutrition.qmd) chapter). Such a patient must be
refed slowly and with monitoring; management comes in the clinical years [@statpearlsRefeeding;
@niceCg32].

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: in a fast lasting weeks, why does muscle protein breakdown slow down instead of speeding up?
As fat breakdown floods the fasting liver with acetyl-CoA, the liver makes ketones, which the brain can
burn readily, whereas fatty acids are a poor brain fuel. Over days to weeks the brain draws most of its
energy from ketones and needs far less glucose. Less glucose demand means less gluconeogenesis, so less
protein is broken down to supply it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why can feeding a severely starved patient quickly be dangerous?
Feeding triggers a sudden insulin surge, and insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium rapidly
into cells. Blood levels of these minerals can then crash, phosphate most dangerously: refeeding
syndrome. A long-starved or very underweight patient is therefore recognised as at risk, and refed
slowly with monitoring.
:::

## Applied fuel metabolism: respiratory quotient, exercise and lipoproteins {#sec-fuel-applied}

The same fuel metabolism can be applied in three further settings: one measured ratio, the respiratory
quotient, that shows which fuel is being oxidised; the choice of fuel during exercise; and the transport
of fat in the blood as lipoproteins.

### The respiratory quotient {#sec-rq}

The respiratory quotient (RQ), the ratio of CO₂ produced to O₂ consumed (see the
[*Energy Balance*](energy-balance.qmd) chapter), shows which fuel is being oxidised. It is about 1.0
when burning pure carbohydrate and about 0.7 when burning pure fat; protein and a mixed diet sit in
between, around 0.8–0.85. After a carbohydrate meal, RQ climbs toward 1.0; deep into a fast it drifts
toward 0.7 as metabolism shifts to fat [@rqValuesStd]. The metabolic switch interactive above shows
this drift from fed to fasted: RQ gives, in one number, the overall direction of fuel metabolism on
the map.

### Fuel use during exercise {#sec-exercise}

Exercise selects fuel along a continuum set by intensity and duration:

::: {.spectrum}
[Main fuel for exercise]{.tree-title}

- The first seconds of effort: stored phosphocreatine
- Short, hard efforts: muscle glycogen, broken down anaerobically to lactate
- Lower-intensity, sustained effort: increasingly fat

[Brief and maximal]{.spectrum-end} [Long and gentle]{.spectrum-end}
:::

The **crossover concept** summarises the trade: as intensity rises, the fuel mix shifts from fat toward
carbohydrate [@brooks1994crossover]. Because glycogen is the limited store, running it down
(**glycogen depletion**) produces the sudden fade that athletes call "hitting the wall", felt by a
marathoner most often around 33–34 km, when the glycogen is spent and only slower fat oxidation is
left [@rapoport2010marathon].

::: {.callout-warning}
## Is there a fat-burning zone?
Gym machines advertise a low-intensity "fat-burning zone", based on a real observation: gentle exercise
burns a higher proportion of fat. It also burns less energy in total. Moving from gentle to moderate
exercise burns more total energy, and more total fat, per minute; total fat burning peaks at a
moderate intensity and falls away in very hard efforts, which run mainly on carbohydrate
[@achten2002fatmax]. For losing fat over weeks, what counts is the total energy
deficit, not the zone a session sat in. The zone is therefore misleading: burning a higher proportion
of fat is not the same as burning more fat.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍳 From physiology to the plate: fuelling everyday exercise
What and when to eat around exercise follows from the map. Muscle glycogen is a limited store, so
topping it up matters, but only when exercise actually runs it low. For everyday activity (a run, a
gym session, a social game), existing glycogen is ample and water is usually all that is needed;
sports drinks and gels are marketing, not physiology (see the
[*Adulthood & Working Life*](adulthood-working-life.qmd) chapter). Carbohydrate loading before, and
fuelling during, help only for prolonged, hard efforts lasting well beyond an hour, where they delay
glycogen depletion: the reason a marathoner carbo-loads and takes gels while a Sunday 5 km runner does
not.
:::

### Lipoprotein metabolism {#sec-lipoproteins}

Fat travels in the blood inside lipoproteins, whose classes are named in the
[*Macronutrients*](macronutrients.qmd) chapter, and the classes are stages of one interconverting
pathway. Dietary fat leaves the gut as chylomicrons (assembled in the gut lining; see the
[*Digestion & Absorption*](digestion-absorption.qmd) chapter); lipoprotein lipase strips their
triglyceride, leaving remnants that the liver clears. The liver exports its own fat as VLDL, which
sheds triglyceride to become IDL (intermediate-density lipoprotein) and then LDL, the main
cholesterol-delivery particle. HDL works in the opposite direction, carrying cholesterol back from the
tissues to the liver: **reverse cholesterol transport** [@feingoldLipoproteins].

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-lipoproteins
%%| fig-cap: "Lipoproteins are not fixed types but a pathway that interconverts as they deliver and retrieve fat and cholesterol."
flowchart LR
  CM["Chylomicron<br/>(dietary fat, from gut)"] -->|"LPL strips triglyceride"| REM["Remnant"] --> LIV["Liver"]
  LIV -->|"exports"| VLDL["VLDL"] -->|"sheds triglyceride"| IDL["IDL"] --> LDL["LDL<br/>(delivers cholesterol)"]
  HDL["HDL"] -.->|"reverse transport"| LIV
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does the respiratory quotient drift from about 1.0 after a carbohydrate meal toward 0.7 deep into a fast?
RQ is the ratio of CO₂ produced to O₂ consumed; pure carbohydrate oxidation gives about 1.0 and pure
fat about 0.7. After a meal metabolism burns mainly carbohydrate; in a fast it shifts to fat, so RQ
falls toward 0.7.
:::

## Failures of metabolic regulation: diabetes, alcohol and hypoglycaemia {#sec-broken}

**Diabetes.** When insulin is missing or ineffective, the regulation of fed and fasted metabolism
fails: muscle and fat cannot take up and store glucose, so glucose accumulates in the blood while the
cells behave as if starving. In type 1 diabetes, the total loss of insulin's inhibition of lipolysis
lets fat breakdown and ketone production in the liver run unchecked, the road to DKA (see
[Physiological ketosis and diabetic ketoacidosis](#sec-dka)). Here the task is to recognise this
failure of regulation; the dietary management of type 2 diabetes comes later (see the
[*Type 2 Diabetes*](type-2-diabetes.qmd) chapter) [@ada2026standards].

**Alcohol on an empty stomach.** Metabolising ethanol floods the liver with the electron carrier NADH,
and that blocks gluconeogenesis. If glycogen is also low, as after skipped meals and a night of
drinking, the liver can make glucose by neither route, and blood glucose can fall dangerously low, a
state called **hypoglycaemia** [@krebs1969alcohol]. Heavy drinking without eating can therefore end in
a hypoglycaemic collapse that looks like ordinary drunkenness.

**Recognising hypoglycaemia.** As blood glucose falls, the counter-regulatory response produces
symptoms in a typical order. Autonomic (neurogenic) warning symptoms come first: tremor, sweating,
palpitations and hunger. They come from the autonomic nervous system, partly through adrenaline and
noradrenaline (tremor, palpitations) and partly through acetylcholine-releasing (cholinergic) nerves
(sweating, hunger), and appear at a higher glucose level, as an early alarm [@towler1993awareness]. **Neuroglycopenic** symptoms, those of the brain itself running short of glucose, follow:
confusion, slurred speech and eventually loss of consciousness [@mitrakou1991;
@diabetologia2022thresholds]. The dependable point is that the autonomic warning comes before the brain
fails; the order of one symptom against another is less consistent than older teaching implied, and
the glucose thresholds shift with context.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: as blood glucose falls, why do tremor and sweating usually come before confusion?
Tremor and sweating are autonomic warning symptoms of the counter-regulatory response, which sets in at
a higher glucose level as an early alarm. Confusion and slurred speech are neuroglycopenic: they appear
only when the brain itself runs short of glucose, at a lower level. The order of the two groups is
dependable even though the order of individual symptoms varies.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: in untreated type 1 diabetes, why are both blood glucose and blood ketones high?
Without insulin, muscle and fat cannot take up and store glucose, so glucose accumulates in the blood.
The same lack of insulin removes its inhibition of lipolysis, so fat breakdown floods the liver with
acetyl-CoA and ketone production runs unchecked. With no insulin to restrain them, ketones rise and
the blood turns acidic: diabetic ketoacidosis.
:::

## Is fasting good or bad for health? {#sec-close}

The question is the wrong shape. Every body fasts every night. After dinner it stores glucose as
glycogen, overnight it spends the liver's glycogen, and towards morning it makes a little new glucose;
throughout, the brain stays supplied, which is why fasting blood glucose is normal after 12 hours
without food. A longer fast escalates into ketosis, which spares muscle protein for weeks. There is no
metabolic catastrophe in a missed meal, and no metabolic magic in a fasting schedule. The main dangers
are clinical: a person with diabetes on insulin or a sulfonylurea (a glucose-lowering drug that can
cause hypoglycaemia), for whom a long fast risks hypoglycaemia; anyone drinking heavily on an empty
stomach; and a severely malnourished person, for whom refeeding is the hazard.

## The Singapore picture {#sec-singapore}

Metabolism is universal, but when, what and how much people eat is cultural, and Singapore's food
environment shapes the fed–fasted cycle in particular ways.

**A culture of abundance prolongs the fed state.** Four features of the local food environment keep
many people in the fed, storing state for a large share of the day:

- hawker centres open from breakfast to supper;
- a strong snacking and late-night eating habit;
- sweet drinks by default;
- a year-round calendar of festivals.

The festivals show the storing state most clearly. Chinese New Year, Hari Raya, Deepavali and
Christmas each bring days of feasting (reunion dinners, *bak kwa* and pineapple tarts, *ketupat* and
*rendang*, log cakes and soft drinks), and fed-state metabolism stores the surplus as glycogen and fat.
Nothing is metabolically wrong: fed-state regulation is working normally. But holiday weight gain is
real: in a US study of the Thanksgiving-to-New-Year season it was modest (under half a kilogram on
average) and was not reversed in the following months, so it probably adds up across the years
[@yanovski2000holiday]. The study was American, but the same physiology applies to Singapore's
festival calendar.

**Ramadan: the fed–fasted cycle, every day for a month.** For a large part of the community the cycle
of fed, fasted and refed states is lived daily for a month. There is no food or drink from dawn to dusk
(~13–14 hours), with a pre-dawn meal (*suhoor*) and the breaking of the fast at sunset (*buka puasa*).
Physiologically, each day runs glycogenolysis giving way to gluconeogenesis, with a shift toward fat
oxidation but not dramatic afternoon ketosis; fasting blood glucose stays within the normal range
across the month [@lessan2019ramadan; @madkour2023metabolomics].

Practical advice follows from this physiology. A *suhoor* built on slower-digesting foods (wholegrains,
protein, some fat) sustains the fast better than a sugary one, and the commonest pitfall is the
rebound: breaking a day's fast with a huge, sweet, fast-digesting spread. A normal-sized meal at *buka puasa* and
rehydrating overnight keep the day's swing gentle.

For someone with diabetes on insulin or a sulfonylurea, this cultural practice becomes a clinical
issue, one to recognise and refer, not
manage. A long daily fast on glucose-lowering medication markedly raises the risk of hypoglycaemia. A
13-country survey put the rise in severe hypoglycaemia at several-fold [@salti2004epidiar], and a
Singapore hospital survey found that nearly half of Muslim patients with diabetes had a hypoglycaemic
episode during the previous Ramadan, over a third had not monitored their glucose, and some fasted on
through the episode [@zainudin2017knowledge]. The
evidence-based response is local too: the Singapore-developed FAST algorithm, tested in a randomised
trial, guides pre-Ramadan medication adjustment [@lum2020fast]. When you see a patient with diabetes
who plans to fast, recognise the risk, advise breaking the fast for a hypoglycaemic episode, and refer
for a pre-Ramadan review (see the [*Type 2 Diabetes*](type-2-diabetes.qmd) chapter).

**Supper and drinking culture.** The local habit of late-night drinking, often after a light dinner or
on an empty stomach, is exactly the setting for the alcohol-and-fasting hypoglycaemia described earlier
(see [Failures of metabolic regulation](#sec-broken)). The plain advice *eat when you drink* is
therefore worth giving, and a friend found confused after a night out deserves a glucose check, not the
assumption that they are "just drunk".

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 How do intermittent fasting and the ketogenic diet work?
Both are popular here, and both work, but through more ordinary mechanisms than their promoters claim.
**Time-restricted eating** (limiting eating to a daily window, as in "16:8") produces weight loss mostly
by reducing total energy intake, and in a careful 12-month trial, adding an eating window to calorie
restriction gave no significantly greater weight loss than the same calorie restriction alone
[@liu2022tre; @decabo2019fasting]. The ketogenic diet likewise works largely through
control of appetite and energy intake, and its nutritional ketosis is not the dangerous ketoacidosis a
patient may fear. (Weighing claims like these is the subject
of the [*Evidence vs Hype*](evidence-vs-hype.qmd) chapter.)
:::

**Diabetes as a national priority.** Singapore declared its War on Diabetes in 2016 [@mohWarOnDiabetes]; in
the 2021–2022 National Population Health Survey, roughly one resident in twelve aged 18 to 74 had
diabetes [@mohNNS2022]. A food
culture that keeps many people in the fed, storing state, together with the ways metabolic regulation
fails, is the physiology beneath that public-health effort.
